name: Mount Escape
description: Combine bridge, elbow escape, and knee-elbow recovery to escape mount with structure.
shortInstruction: Bridge to off-balance, turn to your side, pummel the elbow inside, and recover guard using the knee-elbow connection.
summary: Mount escape uses a sequenced bridge to create space, elbow placement to block the crossface, and hip escape to recover guard or a knee-shield position. The system rewards timing over explosiveness.
whyItWorks: A well-timed bridge loads the opponent's weight onto their hands, creating the window to insert the elbow
The elbow-to-knee connection creates a structural frame that prevents the opponent from flattening you again
Hip escape after the bridge maintains distance and denies them the ability to re-establish high mount
Turning to your side before escaping uses your strongest skeletal alignment against their top pressure
commonMistakes: Bridging without first framing — you waste energy and stay flat
Pulling the knee toward the chest instead of inserting the knee-elbow connection
Turning to the wrong side and giving up the back
Chasing the escape with multiple weak bridges instead of one well-timed bridge with elbow pummel
safetySummary: Escaping mount with explosive bridging in a confined space can cause accidental head clashes
Do not bridge if you feel the opponent has already isolated your arm for an armbar
Relax and breathe when flattened — panic bridging consumes oxygen and makes the position worse

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Mount escape follows a three-step sequence: frame + bridge → elbow pummel → hip escape toward knee-elbow connection. Each step sets up the next — bridging loads weight forward, elbow pummel blocks the crossface, and knee-elbow frames the guard.

decisionTree.condition: Opponent is mounted with both knees on the mat
decisionTree.action: Frame both forearms on their hips, bridge to off-balance them forward, then immediately turn to your side and pummel your near elbow inside.

decisionTree.condition: Opponent posts wide to counter your bridge
decisionTree.action: Re-frame and bridge in the opposite direction before committing to the elbow pummel. Do not force the elbow pummel against a counter — reset and bridge again.
Hip escape away from the opponent while keeping the elbow-knee connection tight. Recover to half guard with a knee shield.

decisionTree.condition: Opponent switches to technical mount as you escape
decisionTree.action: Protect your back immediately by staying on your side and keeping the near arm across your belly. Do not turn away from them.

decisionTree.condition: Opponent flattens you again after the bridge
decisionTree.action: Your elbow pummel was too shallow — focus on getting the elbow past their hip line before committing to the hip escape.

exitStrategies: If you recover knee-elbow, enter half guard and establish the knee shield immediately.
If they turn to side control during the escape, use the frame to keep distance and continue hip escaping.
If the first bridge fails to create space, do not chain multiple weak bridges — one well-timed bridge with elbow pummel is worth ten explosive bridges without structure.

moneyDetails: Mastering the mount escape removes the fear of being mounted — you can train harder and compete more confidently
It is the single most important survival skill in BJJ: everyone gets mounted, not everyone escapes
Competition mount escapes win matches by one point or by resetting to a neutral position where you can attack
fixItFast: If you can't insert the elbow: bridge harder to one side, then sharply change direction to create space on the trapped arm side
If they flatten you again after the bridge: your elbow pummel was too shallow. Focus on getting the elbow past their hip line
If they switch to technical mount: protect the back immediately by staying on your side and keeping the near arm across your belly
